title: Remembering
hookLine: a run in a friend's name, and an old sutta about gifts that reach the dead
tomorrow: what do you bring into a room where someone is dying?

lines: A RUN IN A FRIEND'S NAME.
CAN A GIFT STILL REACH THEM?
cards: People find ways to keep giving after someone dies. A run in a friend's name. A donation to the cause a grandmother loved.
A favorite dish cooked on the day they died, every year. So can you still give someone a gift after they've gone, or is it only for the people left behind?
A short Buddhist text answers yes, and families still chant it at memorials. It doesn't start with rules or rituals.
It opens with a strange, tender picture: the dead, coming back to their old homes, standing outside the walls.

teach.b: The text is called the discourse outside the walls.

It pictures the departed waiting at crossroads and doorposts of the houses they knew, hoping their families remember them. Then it says something blunt: weeping and sorrow and lament don't help the dead.

What helps is giving. When a family gives food, drink or cloth to the community of monks and nuns, and dedicates the good of it to the one who died, the text says the gift reaches them, and they rejoice.
Buddhists call this sharing merit. The good you do isn't a coin you keep; it can be passed on. The text even gives the words a family says as they give: idam vo ñatinam hotu, sukhita hontu ñatayo.
May this be for our relatives; may our relatives be happy. Around Buddhist Asia this takes many forms. A Thai family offers a meal to monks in a grandfather's name.
A Vietnamese family keeps the giỗ, a death anniversary, with incense and a favorite dish. And there's a quiet second gift inside it.
The text closes by saying the dead have been honored, and the giver has gained no small merit. Remembering stops being only an ache, a thing that happens to you on bad days.
It becomes something you can do for them, with your own two hands.

how: Theravada families offer food or robes to monks and dedicate the merit to the dead, often pouring water as the Tirokudda verses are chanted; Vietnamese families keep the giỗ, a yearly death anniversary, with incense, the person's favorite food and a visit to the temple.

o: keeping every object a person owned exactly where they left it
a vow never to speak the name of someone who has died
honoring the dead by giving in their name and sharing the good

games.q: the discourse outside the walls — tap the pairs.
p: wait outside the walls of old homes
don't help the dead, the text says
the gift reaches them; they rejoice

s: in Buddhism, once someone dies nothing you do can reach them
the discourse outside the walls says gifts dedicated to the dead reach them, and they rejoice.
the text says weeping and lament don't help the dead
what helps, it says, is giving in their name.
merit is a private reward you can't share with anyone
sharing merit means passing the good of an act to someone else, living or dead.

games.q: it's the first birthday of your late uncle since he died. your cousins want to do something, but nobody feels like a party. what fits today's text?
o: skip it. marking the day will only keep the sadness going.
give something in his name, a meal or a gift to a cause he loved, and say who it's for.
spend the day looking at old photos and crying together, nothing else.
games.why: the text says lament alone doesn't reach the dead; giving in their name does. tears are welcome; the gift is what you can do for them.

practice: Bring to mind one person who has died, or a stranger whose death you heard about this week. Offer this sit to them: breathe, and let each breath be a small gift in their name.
At the end, say the old line out loud, in Pali or in English: may this be for them; may they be happy.

wordCard.voice: Remembering: giving in someone's name after they've died, and sharing the good of it with them. Grief with something to do.

orig.note: Pali puñña: merit, the good of a kind act, which can be shared.

carryVoice: Carry it: for them, because a gift with their name on it still counts. Day eighteen of thirty, offered.

sources.ref: Khuddakapatha 7, Tirokudda Sutta (also Petavatthu 1.5): the departed outside the walls; lament doesn't help; giving dedicated to them reaches them
